clinical_features.symptoms:
CLINICAL FEATURES 
•
Pain out of proportion to the injury 
•
Pain on passive stretch 
•
Tense compartment  
•
Decreased capillary refill time 
•
Pulses are usually PRESENT. Absent pulses 
may be due to systemic hypotension, 
arterial occlusion or vascular injury 
Late signs – do not delay until these 
appear! 
•
Pallor 
•
Paralysis 
•
Paraesthesia 
 
MANAGEMENT 
TIME SENSITIVE LIMB THREATENING DIAGNOSIS! DO NOT DELAY! 
 
•
Urgent surgical consult 
•
Emergency fasciotomy 
•
Do not delay surgery for imaging e.g. CT angio UNLESS truly necessary 
•
Remove constrictive dressings/casts 
•
Reduce fractures but avoid traction/tight casts 
•
Place limb at the level of the heart 
•
Liberal analgesia – avoid nerve blocks/regional anaesthesia! 
•
Measure intracompartmental pressure if available (can use a-line set) 
•
Consider concomitant rhabdomyolysis and crush syndrome 
 
 
CAUSES 
•
Blunt soft tissue injury 
•
Burns, NB Electrical burns 
•
Casts  
•
Contrast extravasation/other high-speed fluid 
injectors e.g. paint guns 
•
DVT – phlegmasia cerulea/alba dolens 
•
EMG 
•
Exercise – rare 
•
Fractures – common 
•
Haemorrhage (Haemophilia) 
•
Infections 
•
IV/IO infusions 
•
Skin/skeletal traction 
•
Snake bites (NB more likely PSEUDO-
compartment syndrome) 
 
POCUS: may be used as an adjunct to investigate 
cause of compartment syndrome e.g. 
intramuscular haematoma, or pseudo-
compartment syndrome in cytotoxic snakebite 
 
ASSESSMENT 
•
Caused by excessive pressure in a fascial compartment. Leading to decreased perfusion 
•
Most common in tibial/forearm fractures, high-energy wrist fractures, crush injury 
•
Other: restrictive dressings/casts, prolonged immobilization and reperfusion of ischaemic 
limbs.  
•
Document time and mechanism of injury, time of evaluation, level of pain, level of 
consciousness, response to analgesia, neurovascular status of affected limb 
•
AVOID REGIONAL ANAESTHESIA IN HIGH RISK CASES
